nameStory: The Varroa mite gets its name from its genus Varroa, but it's the second part of its scientific name that tells the real story - 'destructor' meaning destroyer. This tiny parasite earned its dramatic name because it literally destroys honey bee colonies, living up to its reputation as one of the most devastating pests in the beekeeping world.
description: The Varroa mite is a microscopic external parasite that looks like a tiny reddish-brown oval disc, roughly the size of a pinhead. These minuscule arachnids are exclusively found clinging to honey bees, where they attach themselves to feed on the bee's body fluids. You'll never spot one wandering around on its own - they can only survive and reproduce within honey bee colonies, making them completely dependent on their hosts.

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Oval, flattened disc shape that looks like a tiny brown seed or scab pressed against the bee's body

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Pinhead-sized, barely visible to the naked eye but noticeable as a brown spot on light-colored bee bodies

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Reddish-brown to dark brown, often appearing as a darker patch against the bee's golden fur

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: Always found attached to honey bees, never free-living; moves slowly when disturbed

idTips.label: Location on Host
idTips.description: Typically clings between the bee's body segments or under the abdomen where it's protected

habitat: Varroa mites are found exclusively within managed and wild honey bee colonies throughout New England. You'll encounter them in backyard beehives, commercial apiaries, and occasionally in wild bee colonies in hollow trees or other natural nesting sites. They cannot survive outside of bee colonies and are most commonly detected during hive inspections in areas with active beekeeping.

seasonality.spring: Mite populations begin building as bee colonies expand and become more active after winter dormancy. Look for them on emerging bees during early hive inspections.
seasonality.summer: Peak reproduction period when mites multiply rapidly in the warm weather. This is when infestations become most visible and damaging to bee colonies.
seasonality.fall: Mite numbers reach critical levels, often causing the most colony damage. Many bee colonies collapse during late fall due to heavy mite infestations.
seasonality.winter: Mites remain active within the clustered bee colony, continuing to weaken bees during the critical overwintering period when colonies are most vulnerable.

funFact: These tiny mites are like vampire mosquitoes for bees - they don't just steal the bee's blood, they actually act like tiny disease-spreading syringes, injecting at least five different viruses that can cause bees to be born with crumpled, useless wings!
confusionNotes: Until the year 2000, Varroa destructor was thought to be the same species as its close relative Varroa jacobsoni - scientists only discovered they were two different species using DNA analysis. To the naked eye, they're virtually identical, so proper identification requires laboratory testing.
contextualKnowledge: The condition caused by Varroa mite infestation is called 'varroosis,' and these mites are considered one of the primary suspects behind Colony Collapse Disorder. Beekeepers consider a 3% infestation rate (3 out of every 100 bees having mites) as the economic threshold where immediate action is needed to save the hive.
compareHints: Since Varroa destructor is the only Varroa species commonly found in New England, it's most easily confused with its close relative Varroa jacobsoni, which looks nearly identical but is much less common. Both are external parasitic mites of honey bees, but DNA analysis is required for definitive species identification. Other bee parasites like tracheal mites live inside the bee's breathing tubes rather than on the outside of the body.
